stories.body:
True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula

I t’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship.

Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.)

Yeoh is enjoyably irascible as Zhao, who goes viral after thrashing a kid in her first competition. Her online fans call her “Grandma Zhao” and the film gently chips away at stereotypes of the older generation; fans assume Zhao is a cuddly elder, while younger cubers underestimate her skill and stamina. Yeoh brings intelligence to the role, but it’s odd that after making Zhao so testy and short-tempered, the film is all soft edges with a squishy centre. Next, can we expect a biopic of the six-year-old Chinese girl who recently set a Rubik’s Cube world record , solving it in just over four seconds?

stories.title: The UAE embraces AI for kindergartners
stories.summary: The country’s approach offers a glimpse of what education could look like if AI literacy becomes as fundamental as reading and writing.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Innovation

The country’s approach offers a glimpse of what education could look like if AI literacy becomes as fundamental as reading and writing.

In September, Henry Price observed a classroom of 7- to 8-year-olds learn about the Stone Age. They discussed and wrote about cave paintings, then put on virtual reality headsets to explore them.

The founding principal of Rugby School Dubai hopes his students will soon study ancient Egypt the same way — reading about it, creating artwork, and then stepping inside a virtual pyramid, or using artificial intelligence to “interview” a pharaoh.

“AI does not replace reading, writing, discussion, or creativity. It enhances them and opens new doors,” Price told Rest of World . “We want our students to be excited by AI, but never [be] passive users. We want children who use AI to ask better questions, not children who rely on it to give them all the answers.”

The United Arab Emirates recently became the first country to make AI a required K-12 subject.

Our goal remains to ensure that any integration of technology is developmentally appropriate and supports meaningful learning.” Saeed Kharbash, CEO of policies, research and programmes at Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority

That puts the country on one side of a growing global debate over what children should learn about AI and when they should encounter it. While the UAE and China are treating early AI literacy as a national priority, some Western governments are moving in the opposite direction. New York City introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in public schools from preschool through grade eight, citing concerns about children’s mental health. Norway has also enacted a similar near-ban for primary school children.

“On one side is the wish to protect childhood, to guard against the addictive pull of some technology, and to raise happy, well-rounded children,” Prince said. “On the other is the fear that those same children could be left behind in a world changing at extraordinary speed.”

The UAE’s approach is not to give young children unrestricted access to AI. Instead, schools teach them how the technology works, where it fails, and when humans should use it.

Teaching kids AI

At Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, a joint initiative between the Dubai government and K-12 education provider Taaleem Education , students in grades one through three are not expected to use generative AI independently, elementary principal James Efford told Rest of World . Instead, teachers use discussions, stories, and role-play to teach them about AI.

In one activity, a teacher might show children something an AI system got wrong, and ask them to identify what is incorrect or unfair. In another, the teacher pretends to be a robot and asks children to give increasingly precise instructions, teaching them how machines respond to the information they receive.

Most UAE schools are treating AI as a form of literacy rather than technical training.

Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority is developing a broader policy framework for digital technology and AI in education. It has a 10-year roadmap to prepare students for rapid technological change with personalized learning.

“Our goal remains to ensure that any integration of technology is developmentally appropriate and supports meaningful learning without replacing the essential non-digital experiences that contribute to children’s growth, well-being and development,” Saeed Kharbash, CEO of policies, research and programmes at KHDA, told Rest of World .

Abu Dhabi’s Department of Education and Knowledge, which is developing the AI education framework for more than 170 private schools in the emirate, did not respond to Rest of World ’s request for comment.

AI is also being used to make classrooms more accessible. Jayda Keer, an inclusion and neurodiversity consultant and former head of inclusion at Dubai International Academy, said schools have used AI to simplify texts for students who struggle with complex vocabulary, translate material for students learning English, and create word banks.

Schools are still cautious

The UAE’s embrace of AI does not mean children are being handed ChatGPT and left alone.

Schools monitor apps and use firewalls. Younger children rarely use AI directly, while older students have restricted access to school-approved apps such as Padlet, Toddle, Canva, Mathletics, Times Tables Rock Stars, ClassDojo, Edmentum, and Epic. At least two schools told Rest of World they use MagicSchool for teacher-directed activities, while one uses Microsoft Copilot.

“We do not currently allow students to use public ChatGPT etc. accounts in school. Nor do we define the programme around a particular AI model or specialist hardware platform,” Efford said.

The government plans to train 22,000 teachers to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning.

22,000 teachers will be trained to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning under the UAE government’s plans.

“Teacher training and support is paramount,” Victor R. Lee, who leads the AI + Education program at the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, told Rest of World . “This is new territory for teachers, and they have their own unique considerations for how they use it and introduce it to students.” At Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, teachers receive initial training, weekly briefings, lesson guides, and prompt banks, as well as support from colleagues. School leaders evaluate how AI is being used through classroom observations, student work, and teacher feedback.

“The emphasis is on developing teachers’ pedagogical confidence as much as their technical knowledge,” Efford said. “When should AI be used, when should it not be used, and how do we make sure it deepens rather than replaces thinking.”

Most countries are yet to commit as deeply. A U.K. primary school trained staff before introducing an AI chatbot to pupils, but there’s no national mandate yet. Estonia has started teacher and student training but for older ages.

China is perhaps the only major exception. Its National Workshop on AI-driven Teacher Capacity Building has reached 103 cities over eight years, and trained 2.97 million teachers, according to the country’s education ministry .

Parents want transparency

Several parents who spoke to Rest of World said they weren’t consulted about the introduction of AI in their children’s curricula, but they all supported it. Still, they raised concerns about transparency and accountability.

“I work in IT, so I see firsthand how fundamentally AI is going to change the workplace and society,” said Gigi Thomas, whose son is enrolled in Year 7 at Cambridge High School. “I would actually be more concerned if schools weren’t teaching children about it.”

Thomas and other parents would rather AI support and complement learning than replace it. “I am also mindful of screen time, online safety, and making sure teachers and parents understand the tools children are using,” said Amna Al Almarri, a homemaker whose 8-year-old son is enrolled at Al Mawakeb school.

Bedour Almarri, who works with the Dubai Land Department, has three children between the ages of six and 12 attending Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej. He called for a clear breakdown of the exact tools being used, how much classroom time is spent interacting with AI versus interacting with teachers and peers, and the guidelines teachers enforce regarding academic integrity.

“While I trust that the school uses educational-grade software with privacy filters, I remain cautious about data privacy, how prompts are stored, and whether children can accidentally bypass safety restrictions,” he said.

Edward Tsoi, CEO and co-founder of AI Safety Asia, a nonprofit focused on governance, public policy, and risk mitigation, said children need to struggle with a difficult sentence, sit with a math problem, and write a clumsy first draft to build the reasoning capacity they would need later in life, including to evaluate AI critically.

We’d draw a hard line between teaching AI and handing children an AI tool.” Edward Tsoi, CEO and co-founder of AI Safety Asia

“If we let AI shortcut that struggle before the underlying skill exists, students get fluency with the tool and no muscle underneath it,” he said. “That’s why we’d draw a hard line between teaching AI and handing children an AI tool, which is commonly treated as the same policy when they’re not.”

Can the UAE’s model travel?

The UAE is not the only place where children are already using AI. Schools in India and Singapore have experimented with AI in classrooms, while South Korea introduced and later withdrew AI textbooks . In Colombia, Meta’s AI tools have interfered with learning rather than improving it.

A recent UNICEF report found that children as young as nine in Congo and Mozambique use AI for homework and want more guidance on how to use it safely.

The UAE has advantages many countries lack. Kenya and Pakistan , for example, are using AI partly to address teacher shortages in schools with much larger classes. Kenya has as many as 68 students per teacher, versus the UAE’s two. That makes the UAE’s approach difficult to replicate.

“Different governments have different value bets, and they’re operating under very different structural constraints,” Tsoi said. “The UAE has a comparatively small, centralized, well-resourced public school system with the political will and budget to back a national mandate. Other large, decentralized systems in the U.S. and much of Southeast Asia, for instance, don’t have that, and a mandate that’s achievable in the UAE’s system could not be implemented as effectively elsewhere.”

Additional reporting by Aarti Jhurani in Dubai.

From batteries and solar panels to drones and satellites, China is building tech capabilities that extend well beyond AI, writes Steve Feldstein in his new book, "Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Big Tech, and the New Shape of Modern Warfare."

stories.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
stories.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February

Published 12 October 2026

US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.

That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.

The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.

As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.

They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".

The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.

Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent Published 1 day ago

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 3 days ago

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 3 days ago

Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.

Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.

The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

stories.body:
The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him

There is a manic quality to Donald Trump ’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.

The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He offered to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies were not interested . He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas.) In early October he started mailing $500 checks to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a $5,000 check if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will go nowhere .

In the face of such setbacks, maybe Trump felt he had to demonstrate he still can get something done. Still, it is somewhat counterintuitive that the administration, in the shape of Vice-President JD Vance, decided to broadcast the one initiative it did manage to bring to fruition: ejecting more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act (ACA) health insurance marketplaces, on grounds that they are not entitled to federal subsidies.

Trump could argue that the cuts fit within the administration’s promised commitment to restore fiscal discipline. But that part of the platform – which came as Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, promised to trim the budget deficit to 3% of US gross domestic product – was never more than a rhetorical feint.

The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees by Trump’s “fraud taskforce”, by contrast, looks a lot like political madness, given the persistent economic anxieties articulated by Democratic and Republican voters across the country.

The savings from the ACA maneuver, estimated by the administration at $2.2bn per year, are chump change compared to the centerpiece of Trump’s fiscal policy – the One Big Beautiful Bill Act from 2025 that is expected to add $4.1tn to budget deficits over the next decade, largely due to tax cuts benefiting the most affluent Americans.

Pace Bessent, the budget deficit is growing rapidly, expected to rise to some $2tn in the fiscal year of 2026, roughly 6% of GDP and some 18% more than in fiscal 2024, the last year of the Biden administration.

Rather than stem budgetary red ink, it’s as if Trump’s objective is to spread misery beyond the 3 million Americans who had to drop their health insurance after the administration last year cancelled subsidies offered by the Biden administration.

The effort is something out of the playbook of Elon Musk’s Doge . His promise to rid the government of “waste” and “fraud” probably caused the deaths of millions of children in the developing world after the dismantling of USAID, but proved largely irrelevant to the task of saving money for the government. It may serve as a masterclass in trolling. But it is not a vote-winner.

Part of Trump’s brain seems to understand this. Trump paid in part for the “beautiful” bill’s colossal tax cut by cutting funding to Medicaid and the Snap food stamp program for low-income Americans. But he engineered most of the cuts to kick in after the midterms to minimize the political cost. The thinking was that lower-income Americans would happily vote for the Republicans out of gratitude for their somewhat bigger tax refund checks this year and tax breaks for overtime and tips (cleverly designed to expire at the end of Trump’s term) and not notice the cuts rushing down the pike on federal programs they relied on.

after newsletter promotion

But the new evictions from the ACA suggest that his brain’s darker side is winning. Indeed, it underscores Trump’s belief that hitting poor people might work for him. Rather than a commitment to sound fiscal policy, a helping hand for American families treading water or an economic platform of any kind, Trump’s latest exercise in “fraud prevention” points to a strategy revolving around punishing people he can define as “bad”. Deep underwater in the polls for his nutty stewardship of the economy, among other things, Trump seems to believe that his one remaining winning card is to do violence against constituencies that his base may not like. Top of the list are immigrants and low-income people. And so it is that ICE is also doubling down, announcing it will hire another 5,000 agents by the end of the year.

The president is on to something. About two-thirds of Republicans believe giving more aid to the poor does more harm than good, according to surveys from the Pew Research Center . Despite the repeated instances of abuse by federal agents, only 19% of Republicans think the Trump administration is doing too much to deport immigrants illegally in the country. The most radical rightwing voters are all in for federal deportations and don’t think the federal government should be responsible for ensuring Americans’ healthcare.

Perhaps Trump’s heart truly lies on the dark side. But doubling down on policies to please the most ardent fanatics in his base ultimately reveals the weakness of Trump’s position. Perhaps even he understands that he has lost the rest of the country . Punishing the poor and the foreign – alongside an unlikely $5,000 Hail Mary pass – is all he has left.

stories.title: Welsh government and Labour strike budget deal with £60m for additional learning needs
stories.summary: The Plaid Cymru-led administration had failed to pass its spending plans during the summer.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Plaid Cymru-led administration has agreed to fund an extra £60m for children with additional learning needs

Published 13 October 2026, 10:00 BST

The Welsh government has reached a deal with Labour on its mini-budget, which had failed to pass in the summer.

Ministers said the Plaid Cymru-led administration had now agreed an extra £60m for the education of children with additional learning needs (ALN).

Labour, which sits in opposition after losing May's Senedd election, had rejected a £40m a year deal across three years, in angry scenes at the Welsh Parliament in the last week of term in July.

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates had demanded £100m this year when the supplementary budget was last discussed.

Reform said the deal was good for Plaid and Labour but not Wales.

Despite the agreement with Labour, headteachers in the NAHT expressed "deep disappointment" at the level of funding.

Drakeford says Labour made mistakes in failed mini-budget talks Published 28 September

The budget will be debated in the Senedd on 3 November.

On Tuesday, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "This agreement reflects what can be achieved when parties across the Senedd work together."

Skates said Labour had "managed to secure a significant cash injection for schools".

"While we still believe the Welsh government should be setting aside more for ALN in schools, it is a welcome first step in dealing with the need to better fund schools."

Plaid Cymru's original mini-budget included £100m for the NHS to bring down waiting times, £55m for childcare and £40m for school repairs.

If the supplementary budget is not passed then the government would have to find other ways to fund its new plans.

Helen Jenner, leader of Reform Wales, said: "This deal may be good for the failed establishment of Plaid and Labour, but it does not deliver for Wales.

"While we welcome extra support for additional learning needs provision, the Welsh government is still sending millions of pounds of taxpayers' money overseas while our public services suffer here at home."

Former Welsh Labour leader Mark Drakeford previously said his party had made mistakes in how it handled negotiations with Plaid over the summer, and suggested there was a case to be made to take the money previously offered by Plaid.

Following Tuesday's announcement, Llŷr Powell, Reform's chief whip, said: "When Mark Drakeford speaks, Ken Skates starts dancing."

Darren Millar, leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd, said: "While we welcome any extra funding for pupils with additional learning needs, this deal is merely a continuation of the same failed budget approach by the Labour-Plaid duopoly that has been letting down the people of Wales for decades."

"The Plaid Cymru Welsh government must stop wasting money overseas that should be spent on public services here in Wales."

It is not known yet if Labour will vote for or abstain on the budget as part of the deal, but a Labour source said the party will allow the supplementary budget to pass.

ALN is the equivalent education system in Wales to special educational needs (SEND) in England.

The Welsh government received extra cash as a result of more SEN spending in England to help schools struggling with debt.

Labour had argued for some of that to be given to schools in Wales.

Rob Kelsall, assistant general secretary of NAHT, said: "While some will undoubtedly celebrate this announcement as a major success, school leaders across Wales are asking a very simple question: what happened to the £322 million that became available to Wales as a result of additional SEND funding in England?"

He added: "What has emerged is a package that falls substantially short of that figure and asks schools to be grateful for receiving only a fraction of what should have been available to learners with additional needs."

The Welsh government's Education Minister, Anna Brychan, said ministers remained in "active discussions" with NAHT Cymru.

She said ALN was a "key priority" for her and she recognised the "significant financial and operational pressures" facing schools and colleges.

"It is my hope that this additional funding, to be used in-year, will alleviate some of the more immediate financial and operational pressures facing schools, colleges, local authorities and support services," she added.

There were angry scenes in the Senedd in July when the Plaid Cymru government brought its supplementary budget to a vote without a deal in place.

Plaid failed to get any opposition support for the package.

Finance Minister Elin Jones accused Labour of behaving as a "destructive opposition" at the time.

Tory Senedd leader Darren Millar said the decision to vote on the budget anyway was "bonkers".

The first minister later said his government had learned "lessons" from the episode, and promised to improve the way his government engaged with others.

It was not clear if the £60m offered in the deal is annual. Anna Brychan said allocation for future years would be part of the preparations for the draft budget for 2027-28.

Talks are ongoing with other parties for the Welsh government's full annual spending plans, which will be voted on by the Senedd early next year.

Of the £60m, £56m will be split between schools and councils - 80% to the former and 20% to the latter.

Another £1.5m will be spent on a long-term sustainability plan, and £2.5m for the further education sector.

stories.body:
Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year

IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’

John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.

Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.

“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”

Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.

Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January .

But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.

In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.

Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”

The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July .

UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.

However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.

It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.

Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer.

The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve , European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.

Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.

The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.

Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.

“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.

The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.

It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.

Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.

He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.

A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.

ZyMix platform has contract with Tencent, which US alleges has links to People’s Liberation Army

A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.

ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.

Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.

The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.

The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.

A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”

China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.

The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.

The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.

The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.

The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.

It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.

A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”

The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”

The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.

In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.

He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”

Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.

He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”

Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”

A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”

ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.

One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.

Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”

Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

stories.title: UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year
stories.summary: The prediction from the IMF comes as final preparations are being made for the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 October 2026, 03:00 BST

The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit the economy in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said.

The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.

Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".

Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.

Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.

Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.

But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies.

"As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said.

The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031.

Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".

The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.

While the IMF's forecasts are closely watched, the figures are only a prediction, a best estimate, of what will happen in the future. Forecasts often turn out to be incorrect due to world events.

Also, the chancellor's spending decisions at the Budget will be based on predictions from the UK's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, not the IMF.

The predictions in the IMF's latest World Economic Outlook suggest:

the UK is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany

UK growth is set to slow next year to 1.2% as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates hit household spending and business investment

UK inflation is expected to average 3.3% this year, and the IMF has increased its forecast for inflation next year to 2.8%.

the IMF said the global economy was "proving resilient" despite the ongoing war in the Middle East, helped by the investment surge in AI.

'Slow bicycle race'

Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".

When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.

Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, told the BBC the IMF's growth forecast was "better than it might have been", but noted that for 2027 it remained "more pessimistic".

"We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are," he added.

Sir Howard said the UK was "a bit of a sideshow" when it comes to the global economy and the IMF was more focused on how much the US is adding to its debt pile.

"That is what is putting pressure on interest rates all over the world and that is what is affecting us as well. Unless the US does something about its deficit, we can expect interest rates to be higher, which of course increases our debt interest costs," he said.

He added that the IMF was giving the UK credit in its forecast for tax rises which it might not end up actually putting through.

Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget.

On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes".

Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".

stories.title: Resisting the Menace of Federal Data Consolidation
stories.summary: In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully consolidated data exposing our private information. This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls. We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters. Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal Privacy Act of 1974. The good news is that many people have stepped forward to resist the federal government’s unprecedented and unlawful data consolidations. Many groups, including EFF, have filed lawsuits to enforce our data privacy laws, and many states have, too. stories.summary: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by since The Social Network , written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast. Sorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that he has borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint . It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged by courageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. Retail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed.

Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout, as first reported by Sky News , external .

But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk.

This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said.

Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees.

The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition.

However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working".

The retailer was sold for £1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.

The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said.

Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout.

Martin Property Group is the management team's "preferred partner", the spokesman said, but the team will "work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that's already taking shape," he added.

However, Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said there are "deep concerns that the business could go into administration" should this buyout fail.

"We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down," he added.

A Poundland source disputed this, however, saying the Martin Property Group is part of the sale process and remains the management team's preferred partner.

As temperatures broke records this summer, sales of air conditioning units soared . But this technology can compound climate change.

Air conditioners pump a gas, known as a refrigerant, around a sealed loop to carry heat out of (and sometimes into) the room. Some of that gas inevitably leaks out over the unit’s working life and when it is scrapped. Unfortunately, many refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases . Worldwide, leaked refrigerants account for roughly one-third of the climate impact of cooling, with electricity used to run the equipment responsible for the rest .

Air conditioning units have different labels. One that has recently been installed in a house or office probably says “R-32”, a type of hydrofluorocarbon (HFC). Older units often say “R-410A”, which is a blend of HFCs. Kilogram for kilogram, R-410A traps around 2,000 times more heat than carbon dioxide. R-32 is still a potent greenhouse gas, but only about a third as warming as R410A .

Scientists have been concerned about these refrigerants for decades. But if you wind the clock back to the 1970s and 1980s, they were more worried about the fact that they harmed the ozone layer than about their impact on the climate. Around this time, researchers discovered that the most widely used refrigerants back then, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were damaging the stratospheric ozone that shields us from the ultraviolet radiation that causes skin cancer.

Read more: There’s something you can do now to cool your home next summer – and it’s far cheaper than air conditioning

Following the discovery of a “hole” in the ozone layer over Antarctica , nations agreed to sign a landmark environmental treaty known as the Montreal protocol in 1987 .

This protocol and its later amendments phased out the CFCs, but allowed, as an interim measure, compounds called hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) that were less harmful for the ozone layer. During the 1990s, HCFCs began to be replaced by HFCs, which don’t deplete ozone at all.

Without the Montreal protocol, studies suggest that ozone holes could have developed over the Arctic as well as Antarctica . Instead, the ozone layer is starting to recover .

Problem solved? Unfortunately not. HFCs, like CFCs and HCFCs, are incredibly potent greenhouse gases. Projections suggest that, without controls, they could add 0.3–0.5°C to global temperatures by the end of this century , a substantial fraction of the roughly 1.2°C of warming caused by human activities .

On October 15 2016, the parties to the Montreal protocol came together in Kigali, Rwanda. They agreed to phase down HFC production in favour of gases with lower global warming potentials (a measure of how potent the gas is relative to carbon dioxide). For the first time, this protocol was used to control gases purely because of their effect on the climate.

In 2014, two years before the Kigali amendment to the Montreal protocol was agreed, the EU adopted rules to phase down HFCs . These rules enable Europe and the UK to meet their Kigali commitments . Since January 2025, new small split air conditioners (units that heat or cool a single room) sold in the UK can no longer use R-410A, an HFC with high global warming potential . Portable units have been barred from using gases with high warming potential since 2020 . The EU now aims to phase out HFCs almost entirely by 2050 .

Beyond looking at labels on air conditioners, how do scientists like us know whether the Kigali amendment is working? The most direct test is to measure the atmosphere.

At Mace Head, an atmospheric research station on the windy west coast of Ireland, instruments have been measuring these gases continuously since 1987. Mace Head is one of a handful of stations around the world measuring these gases at concentrations of just a few parts per trillion.

In 2019, these measurements helped pinpoint the source of renewed global production of CFCs, years after the Montreal protocol’s ban . After a crackdown on illegal CFC production for use in insulating foams , emissions dropped .

The atmospheric data shows that the abundance of HFC compounds has increased substantially in the last decade . But overall growth in their emissions has slowed, and HFC emissions are substantially lower than those projected before the Kigali amendment was agreed .

A 2025 study projected that the climate impact of air conditioning could be similar to, or lower than, its impact today, even with a major increase in demand. But this depends on us meeting or exceeding our Kigali commitments, making air conditioners more efficient, expanding the use of zero-energy cooling measures (such as shading) and switching to low-carbon electricity.

Keeping a close eye on concentrations

Despite the apparent early success of the Kigali amendment, the atmospheric data show there can be no room for complacency.

Last year, scientists showed that emissions of a waste gas called HFC-23, the most potent climate warmer of all the HFCs, are far higher than the emissions of the gas officially reported by signatories to the Kigali amendment . Because HFC-23 is such a strong greenhouse gas, the discrepancy equates to just over half of the UK’s annual greenhouse gas emissions . Researchers and governments are now trying to figure out the reasons for the unexpected emissions .

The contents of air conditioners and fridges have been shaped by the Montreal protocol for almost 40 years. We know where it has worked, and where it needs closer scrutiny, only because researchers keep measuring the atmosphere. The challenge now is to maintain and expand that monitoring, so that the Kigali amendment can continue this remarkable legacy.

stories.title: Who is Navi Pillay, the South African judge who won the Nobel prize? We asked her biographer

stories.body:
International human rights judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. She was honoured for her lifelong dedication to international law and global justice.

To understand more about Pillay and her work, we spoke with Sam Naidu, a feminist and literary scholar with a focus on crime and justice, and the author of a biography of Pillay.

You travelled to Switzerland to interview Pillay in 2009. What lasting impression did she leave?

In the biography, I describe Pillay as a down-to-earth, no-nonsense kind of person with a wicked sense of humour. She was generous with her time and answered all my questions frankly. She exudes strength, integrity and a keen intelligence.

Besides her colleagues at the United Nations (UN), I also spoke with family, friends and former colleagues of hers in South Africa, where I was granted access to her personal archives.

We hail from the same Indian diasporic community in Durban, and I could relate to her life story. As a feminist scholar I chose her as the subject of a book because she was an inspirational black woman who overcame structural barriers to become a pioneer in human rights law, with a global impact.

We had communicated before my trip, but when I arrived in Geneva and she saw me for the first time, she joked, “Ah, but you are only a young one. I was expecting an old person like me.”

Under the warmth and good humour, I detected a steely grit that no foe to justice and no obstacle to human rights can quell. As her stance in response to Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu testifies, this grit seems to have strengthened over time.

Who is Navi Pillay?

I would say that Navi Pillay is an extraordinary woman whose exemplary life has its origins in one of the darkest moments in the annals of human rights and the law. Perhaps her strength lies partly in this provenance.

She was born Navanethem Pillay, with Tamil ancestry. Her grandparents were indentured labourers who arrived in South Africa from India by ship in the late 19th century, a time of British colonialism. They were brought to today’s KwaZulu-Natal province, to work on the sugarcane fields. She was born in 1941 and grew up in a working class home in Clairwood, a suburb of Durban, the fifth of eight children. Her father was a bus driver who earned extra money from fishing. Despite the family’s lack of resources, the value of education was stressed in the Pillay household.

This was a time of white minority rule under a racialised system of separate development. Apartheid was formalised in law in 1948, when Pillay was seven. Black South Africans were given minimal education opportunities, but her school principal recognised her academic smarts and her community helped raise the money for her to attend university to study law. She went on to complete a master’s degree in law and then a doctorate in juridical science at Harvard University.

Read more: Navi Pillay’s Nobel peace prize is a vote of confidence in a global legal order under fire

A staunch anti-apartheid activist, in 1967 she was the first black woman in the country to set up a law practice. One of her earliest cases as her own boss was to defend African National Congress member Phyllis Naidoo , who was under banning orders as a member of the resistance. In 1973 Pillay obtained legal representation for political prisoners at Robben Island prison and, in 1986, co-founded the Advice Desk for Abused Women (now Advice Desk for the Abused ).

The struggle against formal apartheid finally ended in 1994, with South Africa’s first democratic elections. In 1995, Pillay was recommended by former president Nelson Mandela as the first black female judge in the Supreme Court. She joined the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in the same year and in 1999 was promoted as the tribunal’s judge president. She then moved to the International Criminal Court in Hague, after which, in 2008, she was appointed UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

The Nobel Peace Prize is a most fitting acknowledgment. Whether defending political prisoners in South Africa, transforming international criminal law by tackling rape in Rwanda, or denouncing the genocide in Gaza, she has been a fearless trailblazer in the area of human rights since the 1960s.

In August 2009 Forbes Magazine published its list of the world’s 100 most powerful women. At number 64, Navi Pillay was the second African ever to make the list.

She began her career fighting for human rights and justice in apartheid South Africa, but today she speaks for victims everywhere.

As a feminist scholar, you explore crime and violence against women. How did Pillay’s judgments about rape help shape global justice?

Pillay’s interventions at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda changed international human rights law forever. The tribunal became the first court to hold that sexual violence can be an act of genocide. Pillay sat on the bench that presided over the landmark case.

On 30 May 1996, Jean-Paul Akayesu, the former mayor of Taba, a commune in Rwanda, was brought before Trial Chamber I. Fifteen charges of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the Geneva Conventions were brought against him. He pleaded not guilty.

Read more: How can the International Criminal Court achieve justice for women?

During the trial several of the victim-witnesses recounted acts of sexual violence perpetrated against them. But Akayesu was not being charged with sexual violence offences. Faced with this conundrum, Pillay posed a question to the office of the prosecutor:

What are the judges expected to do with the evidence of sexual violence in a trial where there are no charges relating to sexual violence and the main charge is genocide?

As a direct result, the prosecution filed an indictment which later led to the finding that rape may under certain circumstances constitute genocide.

Subsequently, this provision was incorporated into the leading modern instruments of international criminal law. There has rarely been a feminist victory with more real, material impact. As Pillay said :

From time immemorial, rape has been regarded as spoils of war. Now it will be considered a war crime.

I cannot think of anyone else who has infiltrated the system and transformed it so radically from within. Navi Pillay is, after all, the six-year-old girl who stood in a court in Durban and gave evidence when her father was robbed by a colleague. When the robber was convicted but the court process failed to see the money returned, she was left asking, “Where is my father’s money? Is this justice?”

The difference is that now she is 85 years old, with a long and illustrious career behind her. Her question remains but now it has a global focus: “Where is justice for each and every one of us?”

Read more: Trump misses out on Nobel Prize again and imposes new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. What does it mean?

Her life-long quest for justice has won her enemies too, those who would belittle her efforts or criticise her methods, although the ideals she adheres to may be harder to fault. But she appreciates that history unravels in surprising ways.

Who would have thought that Jan Smuts , a white supremacist, would leave the preamble to the UN charter as his lasting legacy to the world? Who would have believed in 1963 that Nelson Mandela would one day be president of South Africa? And who would have guessed that the six-year-old who questioned the meaning of justice in a Durban court would one day win the Nobel Peace Prize?
